newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Good start seen in financial services pact bid.
newsitem.headline: Good start seen in financial services pact bid.

text.p: A good start had been made in talks this week on getting a pact to liberalise the world's megabillion financial services industry by a December deadline, senior officials said on Thursday.

Encouraging comments came from both the chairman of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) negotiating group in the sector and Jeffrey Lang, Deputy United States Trade Representative, who joined a heavy Washington team for the first round.

"I am very much encouraged by the constructive atmosphere," Yoshio Okubo told reporters after chairing the first meeting of the group, which brings in all the some 50 countries currently in the negotiations.

A good start had been made for a "solid agreement" that would be underpinned by WTO rules, added the official, seconded from Japan's Finance Ministry where he is a deputy vice-minister for international affairs.
"There are some favourable indications for this negotiation," Lang told reporters at the U.S. trade mission in Geneva. These included financial market reforms in the works in key emerging economies.
Other good signs were the conclusion in February of a WTO accord on basic telecommunications and last month's agreement to remove tariffs from information technology products.

The new negotiations, which come two years after the United States walked away from an earlier accord when 43 countries led by the European Union agreed an interim pact, face a December deadline for completion.

At the WTO's first Ministerial Meeting in Singapore last December, the now 130 member countries committed themselves to getting what they called "significantly improved market access commitments with a broad level of participation" in a deal.

As the group met in Geneva on Thursday, business leaders representing financial service firms worldwide, including major U.S. and EU-based companies issued a statement saying an accord would bring benefits to rich and poorer countries.
"We believe the chances of reaching a fair, liberalising, non-discriminatory agreement are positive," said one of the signatories, Andrew Buxton, Chairman of the British banking giant Barclays PLC.

But both Lang and Okubo agreed separately that it was a major task to encompass a widely divergent sector -- which covers banking, investment and insurance and related activities -- in an accord satisfying all parties.
And they said time was short, although delegations agreed in principle on Thursday to bring the deadline forward from the year-end, as set in Singapore, to December 12.

Lang said the United States, which argued that offers on the table at the time from advanced developing countries were not enough for Washington when it pulled out in June 1995, was committed to getting an agreement this time.

But he said it was vital to get "a critical mass" of good quality market opening pledges to justify the opening of the U.S. sector -- the world's biggest single financial service market -- to all comers as a pact under WTO rules would demand.
The United States is known to be seeking improvements to what many major emerging economies have on the table under the 1995 interim deal which runs out on December 31.

Among countries likely to be targetted for wider and earlier openings to outside competition across the sector are Malaysia, Thailand and Argentina as well as countries like Brazil, South Korea and Chile who have already announced reforms.
But Lang said he sensed after bilateral talks with several countries this week that there was reluctance among some countries to "bind" domestic reforms -- or fix them as immutable under WTO rules.
Officials said the next meeting of the negotiating group had been set for June 5 with monthly sessions to follow in the autumn when a major drive to get an accord would get under way.
